physics-resonance.caption: Anti-collinear uses (1-r^2)/(1+r^2); collinear uses (r^2-1)/(r^2+1). r = nu_laser / nu_rest.

physics-resonance.name: voltage-from-beta
physics-resonance.caption: beta is converted to V via the full relativistic energy; m c^2 = E_0, q the charge state, e the elementary charge.

physics-resonance.text: If the resulting β falls outside (0, 1) — or voltage_from_beta would return a non-positive voltage — the function returns None rather than an unphysical answer.

laser_frequency_for_resonance(nu_rest, voltage, mass, charge, geometry) is the inverse used by the Estimate tab's [[est-laser|Anchor-to-isotope]] mode: given a chosen acceleration voltage, it returns the lab-frame laser frequency that Doppler-shifts the rest-frame line into resonance. It computes β directly from the voltage, then divides out the Doppler factor.

physics-resonance.name: laser-frequency-resonance
physics-resonance.caption: Anti-collinear multiplies nu_rest by sqrt((1-beta)/(1+beta)); collinear by sqrt((1+beta)/(1-beta)) -- the reciprocal of the seen-frequency factor.

physics-resonance.text: Geometry is resolved by the same normaliser as everywhere else: any string containing anti selects anti-collinear (the CLS default), otherwise collinear.

physics-simulated-spectrum.text: The Estimate tab's plot panel renders a predicted scan in voltage space with generate_voltage_spectrum (cls_estimations/doppler.py). For every hyperfine peak it Doppler-shifts a fixed laser across a swept acceleration voltage and sums Gaussians.
The single user FWHM (MHz, default 100 — see [[est-linewidth-scan]]) becomes a Gaussian standard deviation:

physics-simulated-spectrum.name: fwhm-to-sigma
physics-simulated-spectrum.caption: sigma = FWHM / (2*sqrt(2*ln2)); the simulated peaks are pure Gaussians of this width.

physics-simulated-spectrum.text: The swept acceleration voltage is Vacc = V0 − dV over v_steps points (default 1000), clipped to a 1 V floor to avoid the β routine's NaN tail. Each peak k sits at the rest-frame centroid plus its HFS offset, νc + δk, where νc is the transition frequency plus the isotope shift. The detuning is the difference between the frequency the ion sees ([[physics-doppler]]) and that rest-frame line:

physics-simulated-spectrum.name: simulated-spectrum
physics-simulated-spectrum.caption: a_k are the normalized HFS intensities; nu_seen(dV) is the Doppler-shifted laser at each swept voltage; the sum is normalized to its maximum on output.

physics-simulated-spectrum.text: The y-axis is normalised to its own maximum (y /= y.max() when positive), so the simulated spectrum shows relative intensity, not counts. The linewidth affects only the simulated shape — it never enters the timing math.

physics-voltage-projection.text: When a voltage-merged histogram is fitted in frequency mode, DENIS re-projects the already-binned DAC-voltage bin centres onto a rest-frame MHz axis with voltage_to_frequency_array (cls_estimations/doppler.py). The counts are untouched — only the x-axis interpretation flips.
A single merge-level laser setpoint and harmonic define the lab-frame laser frequency for the whole merged spectrum:

physics-voltage-projection.name: lab-laser-frequency
physics-voltage-projection.caption: laser setpoint in cm^-1 times the harmonic, converted to MHz via c*100/1e6. In code: laser_cm1 * harmonic * C_LIGHT * 100 / 1e6.

physics-voltage-projection.text: Each bin's beam voltage is the cooler voltage minus the scanning voltage, V<sub>beam</sub> = V<sub>cooler</sub> − V<sub>scan</sub>, clipped to a 1 V floor (guarding against misconfigured merge metadata where the cooler voltage is below the scan range). That voltage gives a per-bin β, and the frequency the ion sees follows the same Doppler factor as the rest of DENIS:

physics-voltage-projection.name: doppler-seen
physics-voltage-projection.caption: nu_seen from a lab-frame laser: anti-collinear multiplies by sqrt((1+beta)/(1-beta)), collinear by the reciprocal.

physics-voltage-projection.text: If a non-zero rest-frame reference frequency is supplied, it is subtracted (in MHz) so the output is detuning rather than absolute frequency, matching the Compute_WL(ref=...) convention.

This path assumes a single cooler voltage and single laser setpoint for the entire merged spectrum — that is the whole point of merging into one frequency-domain fit. The user accepted in the [[an-merge-dialog|merge dialog]] that the source files were close enough to share one Doppler shift; Pre-Analysis surfaces a spread warning when they are not, but never blocks.

physics-hfs.text: Hyperfine line positions (MHz offsets from the centroid) and their relative intensities are computed by satlas2's HFS model, wrapped in compute_hfs_lines (cls_estimations/hfs_model.py). The inputs are the nuclear spin I, the lower/upper electronic J values, and the four A/B coupling constants.
Each hyperfine sublevel F shifts from its fine-structure level by the Casimir dipole + quadrupole formula:

physics-hfs.name: hfs-energy
physics-hfs.caption: A is the magnetic-dipole and B the electric-quadrupole constant of the level; C = F(F+1)-I(I+1)-J(J+1). Allowed transitions satisfy Delta_F = 0, +-1 with F=0->0 forbidden.

items: I = 0 short-circuits to a single line at offset 0 with intensity 1 — no hyperfine splitting.
Octupole off: the model passes C=[0.0, 0.0], so DENIS represents dipole + quadrupole HFS only (no magnetic-octupole term).

Intensities normalised to sum 1: after satlas2 returns the relative amplitudes they are divided by their sum, because the [[timing-statistics|timing model]] treats each intensity as a fraction of the total signal.

physics-hfs.text: The A and B constants used here come either from explicit user entry (the [[est-isotope-ab-override|A/B override]] / [[an-model-block|Model block]]) or from scaling a reference isotope — see [[physics-ab-scaling]].

physics-ab-scaling.text: When the hyperfine A and B constants of a new isotope are unknown, DENIS scales them from a reference isotope using nuclear moments (cls_estimations/hfs_model.py). This is what the Estimate tab does for every non-reference isotope unless you tick the [[est-isotope-ab-override|A/B override]].
The A constant is proportional to μ/I, so it scales as the ratio of (μ/I) between the two isotopes (scale_A):

physics-ab-scaling.name: a-scaling
physics-ab-scaling.caption: A = mu * I_ref * A_ref / (mu_ref * I). mu in nuclear magnetons, I the nuclear spin; A_ref is the measured reference A constant (MHz).

physics-ab-scaling.text: The B constant is proportional to the spectroscopic quadrupole moment Q, so it scales as the ratio of Q (scale_B):

physics-ab-scaling.name: b-scaling
physics-ab-scaling.caption: B = Q * B_ref / Q_ref. Q in barn; B_ref the measured reference B constant (MHz).

items: μref = 0 raises a ValueError — A-scaling would divide by zero (this is why the [[est-schmidt-widget|Schmidt widget]] auto-fills a non-zero μ).
I = 0 returns A = 0 (no magnetic hyperfine structure).
Qref = 0 with Q = 0 returns B = 0; Qref = 0 with Q ≠ 0 raises a ValueError — there is no reference quadrupole to scale from.

physics-schmidt-single.text: For isotopes whose magnetic moment is unmeasured, DENIS estimates it from the single-particle nuclear shell model (Schmidt). The orbital is chosen from a built-in shell-ordering table in cls_estimations/schmidt.py; the same code backs the [[est-schmidt-widget|isotope panel widget]] and the standalone [[tool-schmidt|Schmidt calculator]].

ORBITALS lists every subshell from 1s1/2 up to 1j15/2, each tagged with its orbital angular momentum ℓ, total j, capacity, and the magic number it closes (2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126, and the predicted 184). The free-nucleon g-factors are constants:
The moment depends on whether the odd nucleon's spin is aligned (j = ℓ + 1/2) or anti-aligned (j = ℓ − 1/2). For a proton:

physics-schmidt-single.name: schmidt-proton
physics-schmidt-single.caption: g_s is the (optionally quenched) spin g-factor G_S_P*g_s_factor; result in nuclear magnetons.

physics-schmidt-single.text: For a neutron (orbital g-factor is zero):

physics-schmidt-single.name: schmidt-neutron
physics-schmidt-single.caption: g_s = G_S_N*g_s_factor. The neutron orbital contribution vanishes because G_L_N = 0.

physics-schmidt-single.text: The gs quenching factor (default 1.0 = free nucleon; see [[est-advanced-gs]]) multiplies only the spin g-factor, not the orbital part. An invalid (ℓ, j) pairing — one that is neither ℓ+1/2 nor ℓ−1/2 — raises a ValueError. In practice, measured moments lie between the free-nucleon Schmidt lines and the Dirac value; a common choice is gs,eff ≈ 0.7 gs,free (De Groote & Neyens 2022), set via this factor.

The nuclear g-factor is recovered from the moment and spin (g_factor_from_mu_j), and is the bridge into the two-particle addition rule: Here j is the odd nucleon's total angular momentum, which equals the nuclear spin I in the single-particle picture; the general nuclear g-factor is g = μ/I (in units of μN).

physics-schmidt-single.name: g-factor
physics-schmidt-single.caption: g = mu / j; raises if j = 0.

physics-schmidt-two.text: When two unpaired nucleons couple to a total spin I, the moment is built from the two single-particle g-factors via the weak-coupling (Lande) addition rule (two_particle_moment in cls_estimations/schmidt.py).

Each nucleon's single-particle moment is computed from its orbital (see [[physics-schmidt-single]]), converted to a g-factor g<sub>1</sub>, g<sub>2</sub> = μ/j, then combined into a total-spin g-factor and multiplied by I:

physics-schmidt-two.name: two-particle-lande
physics-schmidt-two.caption: g(I) combines the two nucleon g-factors and their j values; mu = g(I)*I. j1, j2 are the single-particle total angular momenta, I the coupled nuclear spin.

items: I must be > 0: a zero or negative total spin raises a ValueError (the formula divides by I(I+1)).
Both nucleons can be protons, both neutrons, or one of each — the proton flag is resolved per nucleon, and the quenching g_s_factor propagates into each single-particle moment.
An unknown orbital name raises a ValueError before any arithmetic.

physics-schmidt-two.text: calculate_schmidt_moment(valence_spec, g_s_factor=...) chooses single- vs two-particle mode from the keys present in the spec dict: {type, orbital} triggers the single-particle path, while {type1, orbital1, type2, orbital2, I} triggers the two-particle path. Anything else raises a ValueError. It returns the moment plus a human-readable description string.

timing-statistics.text: The Estimate tab's beam-time prediction rests on a simple count-rate model in cls_estimations/statistics.py: a per-peak signal rate, an on-peak integration time to reach a target significance, and scanning overhead that converts that into total beam time.
The signal rate of one hyperfine peak is the product of yield, spectroscopic efficiency, and the peak's normalised relative intensity (signal_rate_for_peak):

timing-statistics.name: signal-rate
timing-statistics.caption: S = Y * eps * r_peak. Y is the ion yield (ions/s), eps the efficiency (0..1), r_peak the normalized HFS intensity (sum over peaks = 1).

timing-statistics.text: To reach a required significance σ over a background rate B, the on-peak integration time follows the standard counting-statistics result (time_for_sigma):

timing-statistics.name: on-peak-time
timing-statistics.caption: t = sigma^2 * (S + B) / S^2. Returns +infinity when S <= 0 (an unobservable peak).

timing-statistics.name: timing-curve
timing-statistics.caption: On-peak time t rises steeply as the signal rate S falls (σ = 3, for several background rates B).

timing-statistics.text: The required σ defaults to 3.0 (set in the [[est-statistics|Statistics group]]), not 5. Background B is the effective per-step background rate — for TOF-gated backgrounds it is the continuous rate scaled by the gate/dwell duty cycle ([[est-isotope-background]]).

Scanning overhead (scanning_time) converts the on-peak time into a number of full sweeps and a grand total. The step count is rounded from range/step (floor of 1), the sweep count is the ceiling of on-peak time over dwell, and the total is sweeps × steps × dwell:

timing-statistics.name: sweeps-total-time
timing-statistics.caption: n_steps = round(V_range/V_step); n_sweeps = ceil(t_on-peak / t_dwell); T = n_sweeps * n_steps * t_dwell. Dwell is converted from ms to s.

timing-statistics.text: estimate_isotope_timing applies this to the strongest n_peaks of an isotope (sorted by intensity). In uniform-timing mode it computes one reference timing for a hypothetical full-intensity peak (intensity = 1) and reuses it for every measured peak, rather than timing each peak individually.

physics-isotope-shift.text: The isotope shift is the difference of two fitted centroids; its uncertainty combines several independent budgets. All of this lives in cls_estimations/isotope_shift.py and is consumed by the [[an-isotope-shifts|Isotope Shifts sub-tab]].
For one isotope against the reference (isotope_shift):

physics-isotope-shift.name: isotope-shift
physics-isotope-shift.caption: delta_nu = c_A - c_ref; the simple uncertainty adds the two centroid sigmas in quadrature. All in MHz.

physics-isotope-shift.text: Multiple runs of the same isotope are combined by inverse-variance weighting (weighted_average):

physics-isotope-shift.name: weighted-average
physics-isotope-shift.caption: weighted mean of centroids c_i with weights w_i = 1/sigma_i^2; the combined sigma is 1/sqrt(sum w_i).

physics-isotope-shift.text: When the per-run sigmas understate the actual scatter, weighted_average_with_birge inflates the statistical uncertainty by the Birge ratio (matching satlas2 and the PDG treatment of inconsistent inputs):

physics-isotope-shift.name: birge-inflation
physics-isotope-shift.caption: chi2_red of the inputs about the mean drives b = max(1, sqrt(chi2_red)); the excess sigma_scatter is reported separately from the pure fit sigma.

physics-isotope-shift.text: compute_all_shifts breaks each isotope's uncertainty into four independent components — sigma_fit (inverse-variance), sigma_scatter (Birge excess), sigma_correction (GP drift, see [[physics-gp]]), and sigma_voltage (cooler/laser systematic) — and adds them in quadrature. For the shift variance, the shared-GP correction term subtracts twice the cross-covariance because the sample and reference centroids were corrected by the same GP:

physics-isotope-shift.name: shift-variance-gp
physics-isotope-shift.caption: Var(delta_nu) for the GP-correction component subtracts 2*Cov(c_A, c_ref); similar timestamps tighten the shift, well-separated ones give Cov ~ 0.

physics-isotope-shift.text: cooler_voltage_systematic turns run-to-run jitter in cooler voltage and laser setpoint into a frequency systematic. It takes the standard error of the mean across runs and propagates it through a finite-difference Doppler sensitivity:

physics-isotope-shift.name: auto-sem
physics-isotope-shift.caption: SEM = std / sqrt(N) of the per-run cooler voltage (or laser setpoint), using ddof=1; single-run projects get SEM = 0 and are flagged.

physics-isotope-shift.name: voltage-systematic
physics-isotope-shift.caption: dnu/dV is computed by a 10 mV finite difference; the laser SEM (cm^-1) is converted to MHz and scaled by the Doppler factor nu_ion/nu_laser; the two add in quadrature.

physics-gp.text: Reference-isotope centroids drift over a measurement campaign. DENIS trains a Gaussian Process on time-stamped reference scans to predict the drift at sample timestamps, following van den Borne (KU Leuven PhD, 2025). The implementation is ReferenceCorrector in cls_estimations/reference_correction.py; the [[an-reference-gp|Reference Correction panel]] drives it.
Three kernels are supported (SUPPORTED_KERNELS), each evaluated in pure NumPy at predict time. The RBF (squared-exponential) kernel models smooth slow drift:

physics-gp.name: gp-rbf
physics-gp.caption: eta is the signal stddev, ell the length scale. In code _K_rbf uses eta^2 * exp(-0.5 d^2/ell^2).

physics-gp.text: The Matern-5/2 kernel is slightly rougher:

physics-gp.name: gp-matern
physics-gp.caption: r = sqrt(5)|t1-t2|/ell. The composite 'thesis' kernel is a slow ExpQuad plus a Periodic*Matern52 fast term plus white noise (Eq. 3.5 of the thesis).

physics-gp.text: The periodic component (part of the composite kernel) uses PyMC's convention, which differs from Rasmussen-Williams by a factor of 4 in the inverse length-scale:

physics-gp.name: gp-periodic
physics-gp.caption: PyMC form k = exp(-0.5 (sin(pi|t1-t2|/T)/ell)^2); the ell fitted at MAP time must be applied with this same formula at predict time.

physics-gp.text: Hyperparameters are found by PyMC MAP estimation (find_MAP), with an optional MCMC sample for diagnostics only — the MAP point always drives prediction. predict and cov need no PyMC: they evaluate the kernel directly. The posterior is computed from a Cholesky factor of the noise-augmented training matrix:

physics-gp.name: gp-posterior
physics-gp.caption: K_train + diag(per-obs sigma^2 + sigma_n^2) + JITTER*I, with JITTER = 1e-6 to match PyMC's stabilize(); the posterior mean is the per-sample correction (MHz) and sigma^2 propagates to the centroid systematic.

physics-gp.text: When two isotopes share one corrector, their corrected centroids are correlated. cov(t1, t2) gives the posterior cross-covariance, which the shift formula in [[physics-isotope-shift]] subtracts:

physics-gp.name: gp-propagated-sigma
physics-gp.caption: The shift-correction variance combines each isotope's propagated GP sigma minus twice the GP cross-covariance at the two timestamp sets.

physics-gp.text: The fit requires PyMC and at least 2 included reference observations, each with a strictly positive sigma. PyMC is imported lazily inside fit() so projects still load on hosts without it; only re-fitting needs it. The diagnostic plot reproduces thesis Fig. B.2 (observations with error bars, MAP curve, 1σ and 2σ bands).

physics-fit-objectives.text: The [[an-fitter|Fitter block]] exposes three fit statistics. DENIS only selects the optimiser method, the statistic, and the per-bin error model; the objective itself is evaluated by satlas2 / lmfit. The relevant wiring is in gui/analysis/fitting.py and gui/analysis/binning.py.
The Statistics combo offers Chi-square, Gaussian LLH, and Poisson LLH. Chi-square is the weighted least-squares objective:

physics-fit-objectives.name: chi-square
physics-fit-objectives.caption: sum over bins of (y_i - model)^2 / sigma_i^2, where sigma_i is the per-bin yerr.

physics-fit-objectives.text: The Poisson log-likelihood is recommended for low counts:

physics-fit-objectives.name: poisson-llh
physics-fit-objectives.caption: -2 ln L for Poisson statistics; m_i is the model, y_i the counts.

physics-fit-objectives.name: gaussian-llh
physics-fit-objectives.caption: Gaussian log-likelihood; -2 ln L = sum (y_i - m_i)^2 / sigma_i^2 with a model-dependent sigma.

physics-fit-objectives.text: Chi-square maps to {llh: False}, while Gaussian and Poisson LLH map to {llh: True, llh_method: 'gaussian' | 'poisson'} in the fitter config.
The yerr mode combo on the Source block (_make_yerr in binning.py) sets how the per-bin uncertainty is computed. All three assume Poisson counting statistics:

rows: Default; never zero, with a Poisson low-count interval correction layered on top for y < 10
Textbook Poisson; empty bins (y=0) are floored to 1
Callable; satlas2 re-evaluates the error from the model each iteration

physics-fit-objectives.name: model-yerr
physics-fit-objectives.caption: Model-based mode: sigma_i = sqrt(model) per iteration; in code the residual divides by sqrt(max(model, 1.0)).

physics-fit-objectives.text: The Scale covariance checkbox (default on) scales the parameter uncertainties by √(reduced χ2):

physics-fit-objectives.name: scale-covariance
physics-fit-objectives.caption: sigma_theta is inflated by sqrt(reduced chi-square). Selecting either LLH statistic forces scale_covar off automatically, regardless of the checkbox.

troubleshooting-common.text: Concrete fixes for the issues most likely to bite during install and first run. Each entry names the symptom, the cause verified in code, and the fix. If a problem is not listed here and you can reproduce it, enable the session log first (see [[troubleshooting-logs]]) and capture the traceback.

rows: uv installs but the next command says uv not found
The installer adds uv to your PATH only for the current shell; a fresh login shell has not picked it up yet.
Open a new terminal and re-run install.bat / ./install.sh. The script detects the existing uv and continues.
clstools is not on PyPI. It is pulled from git via [tool.uv.sources] in pyproject.toml (github.com/andry3vi/cls_tools.git), so a missing git or no network breaks the resolve.
Ensure git is installed and reachable. Offline? Clone the repo and repoint the source to your local clone (snippet below), then re-run uv sync.
Windows desktop shortcut opens a black console window
pythonw.exe was not found in .venv\Scripts, so the installer fell back to python.exe which shows a console.
Re-run install.bat full (or uv sync) so the venv contains pythonw.exe, then install.bat shortcut to recreate the shortcut.
Gatekeeper quarantines downloaded scripts, or the file lost its executable bit.
Right-click the .command file and choose Open once to approve it, or run chmod +x ~/Desktop/DENIS.command.

troubleshooting-common.caption: Repoint clstools to a local clone in pyproject.toml, then re-run uv sync.

troubleshooting-common.text: There is no manual PATH edit needed for uv: the installer writes it to %USERPROFILE%\.local\bin (Windows) or ~/.local/bin (Linux/macOS). A new terminal is all that is required.

rows: A numeric field shows a comma decimal (e.g. 1,5) or rejects dots
Each spinbox is created with a US-English locale (QLocale.Language.English, Country.UnitedStates) so the decimal separator is a dot, independent of the OS locale.
Type a dot. If a field still shows a comma it was created outside the helper; report it. There is no global C-locale switch to set.
Auto-Fitter appears to hang or pins all cores
Multi-start parallel leastsq runs Starts fits across Cores worker processes; a high start count on many cores can saturate the machine.
Lower the Starts: spinbox (range 5-500, default 30) and/or the Cores: spinbox before launching. Progress bars per core show it is working, not frozen.
On macOS the window looks cramped or controls are clipped
Native Aqua adds widget padding that clips controls sized for Fusion.
Nothing to do: DENIS forces the Fusion style and a dark palette on every platform at startup, which fixes the macOS layout.

troubleshooting-common.text: The Auto-Fitter also has a Spread: control (fraction of each parameter value to perturb, default 0.30). Shrinking it turns the search into a fine refinement around your current guess; widening it casts a broader net if fits keep converging to the same wrong minimum. See [[an-autofitter]].

troubleshooting-logs.text: DENIS mirrors everything it would print to a terminal into a dated log file, so you can capture a crash even when launched from a desktop shortcut with no console. The log is always on; a Settings toggle raises its verbosity.

items: Every launch writes logs/denis_<timestamp>.log next to the application (format YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS); the newest 20 files are kept, older ones pruned.
The file is a verbatim copy of stdout and stderr, interleaved with a structured, timestamped logger (Python warnings and Qt messages included).
Tick Verbose session log (restart) in File › Settings › General and restart to raise the log level to DEBUG for extra diagnostic detail.

troubleshooting-logs.text: The file is named denis_<timestamp>.log (for example denis_2026-04-28_143015.log, format YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS). It is a verbatim copy of stdout and stderr for that run with no extra formatting; one file is created per launch (the newest 20 are kept).

When DENIS is started via pythonw.exe (the Windows shortcut, no console), there is no underlying stdout. The tee stream tolerates this and writes only to the log file, so the shortcut never hangs waiting on a missing console. Even with no console, output still lands in the log file.
What a crash looks like in the log
An unhandled exception is caught by a crash hook that writes a clearly delimited banner before the normal traceback, so it is easy to find by searching the log for CRASH::

troubleshooting-logs.caption: Crash-hook banner written to stderr (and the log when enabled).

troubleshooting-logs.text: Every session begins by printing a banner with the information needed to reproduce a bug. Copy this block into any report. When the log is enabled the Log file: path is included too.

tool-nist-asd.text: Tools › NIST ASD Browser… is a full in-app browser for the NIST Atomic Spectra Database plus a multi-step laser excitation scheme finder. It is a non-modal singleton window with three tabs — Levels, Lines, and Scheme Finder — under a shared top bar.

Type a spectrum in NIST notation (element + ionization stage in Roman numerals, e.g. Si I, Ca II) and click Fetch: data loads from the local cache when present, otherwise it is downloaded once from NIST and cached as CSV under settings/nist_cache — later sessions work fully offline (Si I ships pre-seeded). Refresh from NIST forces a re-download. NIST data is fetched in vacuum; the Wavelengths: Air / Vacuum combo converts locally with the standard NIST dispersion formula, so the toggle also works offline. A status label reports the loaded line/level counts and the cache date.

NIST leaves the Type column blank for allowed lines; DENIS normalizes blank to E1. If the levels endpoint is unreachable, levels are derived from the lines table (levels that emit no lines are then invisible).

Filter by configuration or term substring, an energy window, or Metastables only (excited levels with no fast allowed E1 decay — candidate scheme starting points), then Apply. The plot combo offers three views:

items: Level diagram — a Grotrian-style view, one column per electron configuration (textbook mathtext labels). Bar opacity encodes the radiative lifetime τ = 1/ΣAki (longer-lived is denser; ground/unknown fully dense), and hovering a bar shows its energy, uncertainty, configuration/term/J, and τ.

Decay channels (selected level) — every decay of the selected table row drawn as downward arrows with width/color by strength, labelled with λ and the branching ratio; the title carries τ. Use it to pick a detection channel.
Lifetimes vs energy — τ per upper level on a log scale; metastables jump out.

tool-nist-asd.text: Add as starting level sends the selected level to the Scheme Finder's starting-levels list and switches to that tab.

Filter by wavelength window, minimum Aki, type (Any / Allowed (E1) / Forbidden), or involvement of a given level (±0.1 cm⁻¹). The table falls back to the observed wavelength for observed-only NIST rows, so λ is never blank. Two plots: a Stick spectrum (λ vs log10 Aki, allowed vs forbidden) and a Line density histogram with an adjustable bin — spectral congestion and contamination risk at a glance. Manual X/Y limit boxes with Set limits / Auto survive redraws.

Searches 1–3-step excitation schemes. Starting levels come from the table (weighted), or tick Auto-discover to use the ground state plus every metastable. Lasers are either named systems — each with a centre, a ± range, and a role (PUMP = never the last step, PROBE = only the last step, ANY), each used at most once per scheme — or one broad wavelength range. Cuts: per-role minimum Aki, a minimum branching ratio for the watched fluorescence channel (the denominator is all decay channels of the final level), a same/different-wavelength detection constraint with a proximity, and a probe orbital filter (e.g. s->p, p->d).

Isobaric contaminants takes a list of spectra (fetched cache-first during the search): an issue is flagged only when a scheme laser can excite the isobar and the isobar fluoresces within the proximity of the detection wavelength. The search runs on a background thread with progress and Cancel.

Schemes are scored as log10(weight) + Σ log10(Aki) + log10(BR) − 5 per contamination issue, deduped by physical pathway (alternative laser assignments collapse into one entry), and ranked. Selecting a row draws the excitation/detection diagram (level bars with configuration and energy labels, one arrow per step with λ and Aki, a dashed detection arrow with the branching ratio, and a red warning title when contaminated) and a full text description. Export results CSV… writes the ranked list, with wavelengths in the currently selected medium.

The browser's state — spectrum, medium, filters, the full search configuration, and the ranked schemes (self-contained, so they restore offline; capped at 200) — persists in the DENIS save file under the top-level nist_asd key and participates in [[exit-prompt|dirty tracking]]. State loaded before the window is first opened is parked and applied on first open.
